title:
Movement and Control of
Biomimetic Humanoid Robots
cite: Portland State University · Agile & Adaptive Robotics Laboratory
notes: Opening, 30 seconds. This dissertation develops and tests components needed to study a biomimetic robot under neural control. It establishes actuator and joint results and selected simulation capabilities. It does not demonstrate harness-free walking. Advisor: M. Anthony Hunt.

title: Four gaps connect actuator mechanics to neural-control experiments
cite: Revision C · Ch. 1, research gaps and objectives
notes: Allow 1 minute. Read the argument in chapter order: predict force across actuator lengths; predict the torque delivered through compliant routes; recover source-grounded sensory evidence; and connect neural circuits to mechanical models with representative verification. These are project-specific gaps, not claims that no related tools exist elsewhere. A research robot is the long-term goal. Each contribution needs its own evidence.

title: This dissertation adds models and tests to an existing robot program
cite: Revision C · Ch. 1; Ch. 6, Model Conversion and Actuator Coupling
notes: 1 minute. Credit the AARL body plan, Morrow’s earlier robot and the Li walker mechanics, Steele’s biomimetic knee, and Deng’s published controller. OpenSim supplies human anatomy and targets; MyoConverter supplies initial conversion; MuJoCo supplies physics; SNS-Toolbox supplies neuron and synapse formulations. My contributions include actuator characterization with collaborators, correction identification, route-design and testing work with collaborators, SADb curation and application, model repairs and audits, and graphical circuit/interface implementations. The 92-actuator model is a modeling scope, not a physical robot completed in this dissertation. Ask me to explain the specific change and evidence rather than implying I invented these packages.

title: Isometric tests measured force across length, pressure, and contraction
cite: Bolen, Elzein, Pang, and Hunt (2026), Actuators · Revision C, Ch. 3
notes: 1 minute. Introduce a braided pneumatic actuator (BPA). Characterization used 10 mm and 20 mm Festo actuators, up to 620 kPa, with 537 force-pressure-contraction observations: 321 for 10 mm and 216 for 20 mm. Resting lengths: 112–518 mm for 10 mm, 300–509 mm for 20 mm. These are isometric measurements. Credit collaborators as coauthors. Valve dynamics and hysteresis are outside this static model.

Filled points are experimental data, the solid line is the new fit, and the dashed manufacturer curve differs most for short actuators. Avoid a universal novelty claim beyond the published scope.

title: Pinned and biomimetic knees separate identification from transfer tests
cite: Revision C · Ch. 4, test stands; four-bar knee credited to Steele et al.
notes: 1 minute. The pinned knee supports identifying transmission effects. The biomimetic four-bar knee has a moving instantaneous center, so load-cell forces must be transformed to that center. Separate force characterization, correction identification, route optimization, and physical tests throughout this section. These apparatus views are existing figure components.

title: Measured actuator length exposes errors in the rigid-route prediction
cite: Revision C · Ch. 4, Fig. FlxPin_preopt; hybrid-method description
notes: 1 minute. The hybrid method substitutes measured actuator length into the characterized force calculation while retaining the joint mechanics. Its closer agreement with measured torque implicates transmission/length assumptions. This is diagnostic evidence, not proof that the force model has zero error. Show where the yellow hybrid points approach the blue measured points while the rigid prediction diverges.

title: The corrected model accounts for length offset, compliance, and wrapping
cite: Revision C · Ch. 4, Improved Torque Model; Appendix C
notes: 1 minute. Chi0 is a constant length offset. Chi1 and chi2 encode effective system stiffness, lumping brackets, fixtures, and the cable winch; they are not independently measured bracket material properties. Chi3 represents lost active length during wrapping. One stiffness pair serves the adopted flexor and extensor configurations. The flexor identification has a flat stiffness valley, so the fitted pair is not unique. The externally imposed redesign overshoot criterion helped choose the adopted pair.

notes: 1 minute. gamultiobj provides the Pareto fronts for identification. Report adopted-member fold assignments: flexor training 48.5 and 41.0 cm, validation 45.7 and 40.6 cm with tendon. The unused 47.9 cm test is a separate post hoc evaluation with encoder correction. Extensor uses three training and three validation tests; three early tests with bracket shifts are excluded. Row 77 of the flexor front and row 32 of the pair-locked extensor front are the picks of record. Route redesign later uses surrogateopt plus patternsearch, a different optimization task.

title: The earlier single-actuator flexor falls short of its human target
cite: Revision C · Ch. 4, Fig. FlxGrp, panel B

title: The corrected 620 kPa prediction still exceeds many measured flexor torques
cite: Knee-torque paper · Fig. Flx20mm, panel B; unchanged MATLAB calculation

title: SADb links sensory-feedback literature to inspectable source records
section: Sensory Afferent Database: gap and contribution
cite: Revision C · Ch. 5, The Resource; SADb application snapshot
notes: 1 minute. Gap: controller-design evidence is dispersed across species, preparations, tasks, and papers. I curate linked paper, pathway, model, review, and recorder records and build the read-only browser application. Latest distributed snapshot: 1,393 total records, including 943 papers and 450 other linked records. This is a curated research collection, not a systematic review. Offline embedded data support searching, pivoting, and citation exploration; the separate online-search tab requires connectivity. The existing screenshot illustrates the application, not a benchmark of retrieval accuracy.

title: SADb exposes classification coverage without supplying controller gains
section: Sensory Afferent Database: use and limits
cite: Revision C · Ch. 5, Fig. sadb_pivot and Use in Neural-Controller Design
notes: 1 minute. A pivot cell counts tagged papers, not neurons or independent physiological observations. A paper can appear in more than one cell. Selecting a cell retrieves the underlying records. Afferent classes Ia, Ib, and II denote spindle-primary, tendon-organ, and spindle-secondary channels. Their properties depend on preparation and task. Source conditions, sign, and phase guide interpretation; translating them into robot encoders and gains remains an explicit design and verification step. AI-assisted drafting does not count as scientific curation without source checking. The corpus is uneven and not exhaustively classified.

title: The initial AnimatLab controller used one rhythm generator for suspended stepping
cite: Revision C · Ch. 6, The AnimatLab Bipedal Walker; Li (2017), Deng (2019), Bolen (2021)
notes: 1 minute. Morrow and I combined Li’s mechanics with Deng’s two-level controller. The initial controller had ONE rhythm generator controlling both sides and a separate pattern-formation layer. I added a passive toe joint. Suspended alternating activity and stepping-like movement preceded subsequent feedback and bilateral-RG extensions. Hand tuning did not achieve weight-bearing walking. Do not attribute this earlier result to the later two-RG network. The body view and left-joint traces are the historical AnimatLab reference images. The angle units are not explicit in the source capture, so no numeric amplitude is asserted or converted.

title: I later interconnected separate left and right rhythm generators
cite: Revision C · Ch. 6, The AnimatLab Bipedal Walker
notes: 45 seconds. RG means rhythm generator. This editable conceptual schematic summarizes the documented bilateral architecture, not the full connectome. I constructed right-side subsystems from the left organization and connected the two RGs through commissural pathways. No walking result follows from assembly alone. The initial suspended stepping preceded this extension. Published Deng architecture underlies the controller; the bilateral extension is my contribution.

title: My interfaces connect existing mechanics and neural formulations
cite: Revision C · Ch. 6, Model Conversion and Graphical Circuit Construction
notes: 1 minute. OpenSim and MyoConverter supply geometry and initial conversion; MuJoCo supplies physics; SNS-Toolbox supplies conductance-based neural equations. My additions repair and audit custom muscle paths and joint signs, couple the quasi-static BPA-force model, and implement editable Simulink blocks and circuit interfaces. Neural and mechanical models exchange signals every 2 ms. There is no new neuron formulation or demonstrated integrated valve dynamics. Mechanical imports remain distinct from standalone reflex demonstrations. No Hunt/Young library comparison or speed superiority is claimed.

title: The graphical library implements defined Ia and Ib reflex pathways
cite: Revision C · Ch. 6, Fig. simulink_reflex_topology
notes: 1 minute. Reduced-order antagonist knee model. Ia spindle excitation drives its homonymous motor pool and reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist. Ib tendon-organ input inhibits the homonymous pool in this demonstration. These are chosen circuit rules, not a universal claim about Ib function. Mechanical parameters and generic BPA-block parameters remain provisional. In the separate beverage-arm demonstration, reflex enabled sag was 2.00 degrees versus 7.85 degrees disabled. That reduced model does not establish reflex control of imported full-body mechanisms.

title: Matched rhythm-core implementations reproduce the same driven bursts
cite: Revision C · Ch. 6, Fig. w2l_crossengine; matched NumPy and Simulink protocol
notes: 1.5 minutes. The contact-driven W2L rhythm-core test receives matched inputs. Ten expected bursts appear, burst period 1.000 s, full-trace correlation at least 0.99996, with a residual 2 ms lag of one solver step. Removing phasic heel-contact inputs makes both realizations latch. This agreement is scoped to the circuit and protocol. It is neither autonomous oscillation proof nor walking verification. The separate 92-actuator tonic-drive test has a discrepancy and follows next.

title: The bridge exchanges signals while full-network dynamics still disagree
cite: Revision C · Ch. 6, Closed-Loop Model Coupling and capability table
notes: 1 minute. The bridge was checked against independent Python integration with single-muscle activation, different control rates, and sensor readback. Readback is bit-exact over the scored window. The exported neural network drove all 92 actuators for 5 seconds. However, tonic drive caused the Simulink realization to settle while the NumPy reference oscillated. Transfer of tuned controller parameters remains unresolved. Do not generalize the rhythm-core agreement to the full network. Hardware deployment and unsupported walking remain future work.

title: The evidence supports static torque capacity and specific simulation interfaces
cite: Revision C · Chs. 3–7; final flexor MATLAB reduction, 23 October 2026
notes: 1 minute. Return to the four original gaps. Force: supported by characterized lengths and isometric data. Torque: identified corrections improve held-out predictions and redesigned routes have physical tests. Sensory evidence: searchable, linked, partially curated literature resource. Neural tools: matched circuit and interface checks, with explicit full-network discrepancy. Neither static isometric capacity nor supported stepping demonstrates a walking robot. No harness-free walking exists in the program records.

title: Matched-pressure tests and controller reconciliation are the next checks
cite: Revision C · Ch. 7; Ch. 6, remaining limits
notes: 45 seconds. The next experiments address the uncertainty exposed by the results: matched-pressure torque holds over the range, and diagnosing numerical/network differences before transferring tuned control. The dashed hardware path in this existing pipeline is proposed. Do not present a Jetson deployment, completed valve dynamics, or whole-body walking as achieved. Physical pulley tests and simultaneous biarticular verification are future work.
